topics.title: Data Types
topics.content_html:
JavaScript has seven primitive types. Objects, arrays, and functions are reference values.

const ratio = 3.14;

topics.title: Gotchas
topics.content_html:
# Mutable default — shared across calls
def append(item, bucket=[]):   # BAD
    bucket.append(item); return bucket

def append(item, bucket=None):  # GOOD
    if bucket is None: bucket = []
    bucket.append(item); return bucket

# is vs ==
a is b          # identity
a == b          # equality

# Late-binding closures
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
funcs[0]()      # 2 — all see final i
funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]  # capture

# Generator exhaustion
g = (x*x for x in range(3))
list(g); list(g)  # second is []

# Prefer specific exceptions over bare except
Common mistake Mutable defaults and late-binding closures are classic traps. Prefer None defaults and default-arg capture in lambdas.

topics.title: Ownership & Borrowing
topics.content_html:
Every value has one owner. Non-Copy assignment moves; the old binding is invalid.

let s1 = String::from("hello");
let s2 = s1;                  // move — s1 invalid
println!("{s2}");

let n1 = 5;                   // i32 is Copy
let n2 = n1;                  // both valid

fn print_len(s: &String) -> usize { s.len() }
print_len(&s);                // borrow, s still valid

fn add_world(s: &mut String) { s.push_str(", world"); }
let mut s = String::from("hello");
add_world(&mut s);

// either one &mut OR any number of & — never both
let s3 = s2.clone();
★ Ownership defaults Prefer borrowing (&T / &mut T) over cloning. Own with T only when you need exclusive ownership.
Need ownership? │ ├─ no -> borrow │ ├─ read-only -> &T │ └─ mutate -> &mut T └─ yes -> move T └─ shared ownership? -> Arc<T> (or Rc<T> single-threaded)
Common mistake Don't clone() just to silence the borrow checker — prefer a borrow or a redesign.
topics.search_keywords: move borrow reference mut clone drop

topics.title: Error Handling
topics.content_html:
No exceptions. Recoverable: Result<T, E>. Unrecoverable: panic!.

fn divide(a: f64, b: f64) -> Result<f64, String> {
    if b == 0.0 { return Err("Cannot divide by zero!".into()); }
    Ok(a / b)
}

match divide(10.0, 0.0) {
    Ok(r) => println!("Result: {r}"),
    Err(e) => println!("{e}"),
}

fn read_number() -> Result<i32, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let s = std::fs::read_to_string("num.txt")?;
    let n: i32 = s.trim().parse()?;
    Ok(n)
}

result.unwrap_or(0);
Some(4).map(|n| n * 2);
★ Error handling defaults Result<T, E> recoverable · Option<T> absence · ? to propagate · Prefer unwrap_or / ok_or over bare unwrap() in libraries.

topics.title: Gotchas
topics.content_html:
// Unnecessary clone — prefer a borrow
let s2 = s1.clone();   // only when you need ownership

// Borrowing across mutation
let r = &v[0];
v.push(1);             // error while r lives

// unwrap in libraries
value.unwrap();        // prefer ? / unwrap_or / ok_or

// Blocking inside async
std::thread::sleep(...);  // use tokio::time::sleep

// Mutex poisoning — a panic while holding the lock poisons it;
// later .lock() calls return Err instead of panicking silently
let guard = match mutex.lock() {
    Ok(g) => g,
    Err(poisoned) => poisoned.into_inner(), // recover the data anyway
};

// Prefer &T / &mut T; Arc only for shared ownership across threads
Common mistake clone() and unwrap() silence the compiler but hide design issues. Prefer borrows and ? propagation.

topics.title: Pointers & Smart Pointers
topics.content_html:
int* p = nullptr;
p = new int(42);  delete p;

auto up = std::make_unique<int>(42);
auto up2 = std::move(up);

auto sp = std::make_shared<int>(7);
std::weak_ptr<int> wp = sp;
if (auto locked = wp.lock()) { /* use */ }

std::move(x);  std::forward<T>(x);
★ Ownership defaults std::unique_ptr<T> — default exclusive ownership · std::shared_ptr<T> — only when shared ownership is required · std::weak_ptr<T> — non-owning observer
Need ownership? │ ├─ exclusive -> unique_ptr<T> └─ shared ├─ owning -> shared_ptr<T> └─ observe only -> weak_ptr<T>
Common mistake std::move(x) only casts to an rvalue — it does not move by itself. Prefer RAII / smart pointers over raw new/delete.

topics.title: Special Member Functions & Rules
topics.content_html:
Foo();  Foo(const Foo&);  Foo(Foo&&);
Foo& operator=(const Foo&);  Foo& operator=(Foo&&);
~Foo();
Foo() = default;
Foo(const Foo&) = delete;
★ Preferred design Rule of Zero > Rule of Five > Rule of Three. Let the compiler generate special members; manage resources with smart pointers and STL containers.

Rule of Zero (preferred)

class Widget {
  std::string name_;
  std::vector<int> data_;
  std::unique_ptr<Impl> impl_;

topics.title: Selected Design Patterns
topics.content_html:
// Meyer's singleton (thread-safe since C++11)
class Logger {
  Logger() = default;
public:
  static Logger& instance() {
    static Logger inst;
    return inst;
  }
  Logger(const Logger&) = delete;
};
// Prefer composition; RAII is the core pattern

topics.title: Gotchas
topics.content_html:
// Dangling string_view
std::string_view sv = std::string("temp");  // BAD

// Iterator invalidation
auto it = v.begin();
v.push_back(x);   // may invalidate it

// Object slicing
Base b = Derived{};

// std::move is only a cast
auto y = std::move(x);  // move ctor does the work

// Prefer unique_ptr; shared_ptr only for true shared ownership
void f(const std::vector<int>& v);  // avoid accidental copies

// span / string_view do not own data
Common mistake std::move is a cast. Prefer RAII and unique_ptr.

topics.title: Records C# 9+
topics.content_html:

    public required string Id { get; init; }
    public decimal Total { get; init; }
}
When to use record — value-oriented data with value equality · class — identity / behavior · struct / record struct — small value types
★ Value-oriented data Prefer record for immutable DTOs and domain values.

topics.title: LINQ
topics.content_html:
using System.Linq;
var adults = people
    .Where(p => p.Age >= 18)
    .OrderBy(p => p.LastName)
    .Select(p => p.Name)
    .ToList();

var q = from p in people
        where p.Age >= 18
        orderby p.LastName
        select p.Name;

// Any, All, Count, First, FirstOrDefault, Select, Where,
// OrderBy, GroupBy, Join, Aggregate, ToList, ToDictionary
Common mistake LINQ is deferred — runs when enumerated. Multiple enumeration can repeat work or hit a disposed context. Materialize with ToList() / ToArray() when needed.

topics.title: Async / Await
topics.content_html:
public async Task<string> FetchAsync(string url) {
    using var client = new HttpClient();
    return await client.GetStringAsync(url);
}
public async Task ProcessManyAsync(IEnumerable<string> urls) {
    string[] results = await Task.WhenAll(urls.Select(FetchAsync));
}
public async ValueTask<int> GetCachedAsync() { ... }
public async IAsyncEnumerable<int> GenerateAsync() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        await Task.Delay(100);
        yield return i;
    }
}
await foreach (var n in GenerateAsync()) { ... }
Common mistake Avoid .Result / .Wait() — can deadlock. Prefer await. Pass CancellationToken. Prefer async Task over async void (except event handlers).

topics.title: Spans, Memory & Performance
topics.content_html:
Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[256];
Memory<byte> mem = new byte[1024];
var pool = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared;
byte[] buf = pool.Rent(4096);
try { ... } finally { pool.Return(buf); }
ref struct Utf8Parser { ... }
When to use Span<T> — stack-only, high-perf slices · Memory<T> — heap-compatible, usable across await · Prefer them to avoid allocations in hot paths.

topics.title: Gotchas
topics.content_html:
// .Result / .Wait() — can deadlock
var x = FetchAsync().Result;   // BAD
var x = await FetchAsync();    // GOOD

// async void — only for event handlers
async Task WorkAsync() { }     // prefer

// LINQ multiple enumeration
var q = items.Where(...);
var list = q.ToList();         // materialize once

// Nullable suppression — use sparingly
string s = maybe!;

// Avoid boxing in hot paths — allocates on the heap
object o = 42;          // BAD in a loop: boxes every iteration
List<int> nums = [];    // GOOD: generics avoid boxing entirely
Common mistake Prefer await over .Result/.Wait(). Materialize LINQ with ToList() when enumerating more than once.
